# Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) — Clinical Overview

Title: Acute Coronary Syndrome Clinical Guide
Document Type: clinical_guideline

## Definition

Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) encompasses a range of conditions associated with sudden reduction or blockage of blood flow to the heart. It includes:
- ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI)
- Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI)
- Unstable angina

## Risk Factors

## Risk Factors

Major risk factors for ACS include:
- Age (men ≥ 45, women ≥ 55)
- Hypertension
- Diabetes mellitus
- Dyslipidemia (elevated LDL, low HDL)
- Smoking
- Family history of premature coronary artery disease
- Obesity
- Sedentary lifestyle

## Clinical Presentation

Typical symptoms:
- Chest pain or pressure (substernal, may radiate to left arm, jaw, or back)
- Diaphoresis (sweating)
- Nausea or vomiting
- Dyspnea
- Palpitations
- Feeling of impending doom

Atypical presentations (more common in women, elderly, diabetic patients):
- Epigastric pain
- Fatigue
- Isolated dyspnea
- Syncope

## Laboratory Findings

Key biomarkers:
- Troponin I or T: Elevated above 99th percentile indicates myocardial injury. Serial measurements recommended. Troponin is the most sensitive and specific biomarker.
- CK-MB: Less specific than troponin; rises 4-6 hours after onset.
- BNP/NT-proBNP: May be elevated indicating heart failure.

Other findings:
- Possible elevated glucose (stress hyperglycemia)
- Elevated WBC (inflammatory response)
- Elevated CRP
- Possible renal function changes (creatinine)

## Electrocardiographic Findings

- ST elevation: STEMI
- ST depression: NSTEMI or unstable angina
- T-wave inversions
- New left bundle branch block
- Q waves (established infarction)

## Imaging

## Imaging

- Chest X-ray: May show cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema
- Echocardiography: Wall motion abnormalities, ejection fraction assessment
- Coronary angiography: Definitive for identifying coronary occlusion

## Differential Diagnosis

Conditions that may present similarly to ACS:
- Pulmonary embolism
- Aortic dissection
- Pericarditis
- Myocarditis
- Pneumothorax
- Musculoskeletal chest pain
- Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)
- Panic disorder

## Complications

## Complications

- Heart failure
- Cardiogenic shock
- Cardiac arrhythmias
- Mitral regurgitation
- Ventricular septal rupture
- Pericarditis

# Complete Blood Count (CBC) — Interpretation Guide

Title: CBC Interpretation Guide
Document Type: educational

## Overview

The complete blood count (CBC) is one of the most commonly ordered laboratory tests. It provides valuable information about the three major cell lines in blood: red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.

## White Blood Cell Count (WBC)

Normal range: 4,500–11,000 cells/μL

### Leukocytosis (WBC > 11,000/μL)

### Leukocytosis (WBC > 11,000/μL)

Common causes:
- Bacterial infection (most common)
- Inflammatory conditions
- Stress response (physical or emotional)
- Medications (corticosteroids)
- Leukemia and myeloproliferative disorders
- Tissue necrosis
- Smoking

### Leukopenia (WBC < 4,500/μL)

Common causes:
- Viral infections
- Bone marrow suppression
- Autoimmune conditions
- Medications (chemotherapy, certain antibiotics)
- Severe sepsis (late stage)
- Nutritional deficiencies

## Hemoglobin / Hematocrit

## Hemoglobin / Hematocrit

Normal hemoglobin: Men 13.5–17.5 g/dL, Women 12.0–16.0 g/dL

### Anemia (Low Hemoglobin)

Classification by MCV:
- Microcytic (MCV < 80 fL): Iron deficiency, thalassemia, chronic disease
- Normocytic (MCV 80–100 fL): Acute blood loss, chronic kidney disease, anemia of chronic disease
- Macrocytic (MCV > 100 fL): B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, liver disease, hypothyroidism

### Polycythemia (High Hemoglobin)

### Polycythemia (High Hemoglobin)

Causes:
- Polycythemia vera
- Chronic hypoxia (COPD, high altitude)
- Dehydration (relative polycythemia)

## Platelet Count

Normal range: 150,000–400,000/μL

### Thrombocytopenia (Platelets < 150,000/μL)

Common causes:
- Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)
- Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
- Liver disease (hypersplenism)
- Medication-induced (heparin — HIT)
- Bone marrow disorders
- Severe infections

### Thrombocytosis (Platelets > 400,000/μL)

### Thrombocytosis (Platelets > 400,000/μL)

Common causes:
- Reactive (infection, inflammation, iron deficiency)
- Essential thrombocythemia
- Post-splenectomy

## Clinical Significance

The CBC should always be interpreted in the clinical context. Isolated laboratory values may be misleading without considering:
- Patient symptoms and history
- Medications
- Acute vs. chronic changes
- Trends over time
- Other laboratory results

# Chest X-Ray Interpretation — Educational Guide

Title: Chest X-Ray Interpretation Guide
Document Type: educational

## Systematic Approach

A systematic approach to chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation ensures no pathology is missed. Use the ABCDE approach:

### A — Airway
- Trachea: Midline or deviated?
- Tracheal deviation suggests tension pneumothorax, large pleural effusion, or mediastinal mass
- Carina: Normal bifurcation angle

### B — Bones
- Rib fractures
- Lytic or blastic lesions
- Cervical spine alignment
- Shoulder joints

### C — Cardiac
- Heart size: Cardiothoracic ratio (CTR) < 0.5 on PA film is normal
- Cardiomegaly: CTR > 0.5
- Heart borders: Right (right atrium), Left (left ventricle)
- Aortic knob
- Pericardial effusion (water bottle sign)

### D — Diaphragm
- Right hemidiaphragm normally higher than left
- Flattened diaphragm: Hyperinflation (COPD, asthma)
- Elevated hemidiaphragm: Phrenic nerve palsy, hepatomegaly, subphrenic abscess
- Free air under diaphragm: Pneumoperitoneum (perforation)

### E — Everything else (Lung fields, soft tissue, lines/tubes)

## Common Lung Pathologies on CXR

## Common Lung Pathologies on CXR

### Consolidation
- Opacification of lung parenchyma with air bronchograms
- Causes: Pneumonia (most common), pulmonary hemorrhage, organizing pneumonia
- Lobar pattern: Typical bacterial pneumonia
- Patchy/bilateral: Atypical pneumonia, aspiration

### Pleural Effusion
- Blunting of costophrenic angle (> 200 mL needed on PA film)
- Meniscus sign
- Massive: Opacification of hemithorax with mediastinal shift away
- Causes: Heart failure, infection (parapneumonic/empyema), malignancy, PE

### Pneumothorax
- Visible visceral pleural line
- Absence of lung markings beyond the pleural line
- Tension pneumothorax: Mediastinal shift away, flattened diaphragm

### Interstitial Patterns
- Reticular: Pulmonary fibrosis, interstitial lung disease
- Nodular: Miliary TB, metastases, sarcoidosis
- Ground glass: Viral pneumonia, PCP, early ARDS

### Mass Lesions
- Solitary pulmonary nodule: < 3 cm
- Lung mass: > 3 cm (higher malignancy concern)
- Evaluate: Shape, margins, calcification, cavitation

### Pulmonary Edema
- Cardiogenic: Bilateral, perihilar "bat wing" distribution, cephalization of vessels, Kerley B lines, pleural effusions
- Non-cardiogenic (ARDS): Bilateral, peripheral, without cephalization

## Limitations
- CXR has limited sensitivity for small nodules, early interstitial disease, and PE
- CT is superior for detailed evaluation
- Clinical correlation is always essential

# Glucose Metabolism and Diabetes — Clinical Overview

Title: Glucose Metabolism and Diabetes Overview
Document Type: educational

## Blood Glucose

### Fasting Blood Glucose
- Normal: < 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L)
- Pre-diabetes: 100–125 mg/dL (5.6–6.9 mmol/L)
- Diabetes: ≥ 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L)

### Random Blood Glucose
- Diabetes: ≥ 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) with symptoms

### HbA1c
- Normal: < 5.7%
- Pre-diabetes: 5.7–6.4%
- Diabetes: ≥ 6.5%

## Hyperglycemia

## Hyperglycemia

### Causes
- Diabetes mellitus (type 1 or type 2)
- Stress hyperglycemia (acute illness, surgery, trauma)
- Medications (corticosteroids, thiazide diuretics)
- Cushing syndrome
- Acromegaly
- Pancreatitis
- Parenteral nutrition

### Clinical Significance
Stress hyperglycemia in hospitalized patients is common and associated with worse outcomes, even without a prior diagnosis of diabetes. It may occur during:
- Acute infections (pneumonia, sepsis)
- Myocardial infarction
- Stroke
- Trauma

## Hypoglycemia

### Definition
Blood glucose < 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L)

### Causes
- Insulin or sulfonylurea use
- Missed meals
- Excessive alcohol
- Adrenal insufficiency
- Hepatic failure
- Insulinoma
- Sepsis

### Symptoms
- Autonomic: Sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger
- Neuroglycopenic: Confusion, drowsiness, seizures, coma

## Diabetic Emergencies

metadata.title: Glucose Metabolism and Diabetes — Clinical Overview

content:
## Diabetic Emergencies

### Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
- More common in type 1 diabetes
- Characterized by hyperglycemia, ketosis, metabolic acidosis
- Presents with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing
- Lab findings: Glucose > 250, pH < 7.3, bicarbonate < 18, positive ketones

### Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS)
- More common in type 2 diabetes
- Severe hyperglycemia (> 600 mg/dL) without significant ketosis
- Profound dehydration
- Altered mental status

## Complications of Chronic Hyperglycemia
- Retinopathy
- Nephropathy
- Neuropathy (peripheral and autonomic)
- Cardiovascular disease
- Peripheral arterial disease
- Increased infection risk

# Inflammatory Markers — Clinical Interpretation

Title: Inflammatory Markers Guide
Document Type: educational

## C-Reactive Protein (CRP)

### Overview
CRP is an acute-phase reactant produced by the liver in response to inflammation. It is a non-specific marker that rises rapidly (within 6-8 hours) in response to infection, tissue injury, or inflammation.

### Normal Values
- Normal: < 10 mg/L
- Mild elevation: 10–40 mg/L
- Moderate elevation: 40–100 mg/L
- Severe elevation: > 100 mg/L

### Clinical Interpretation

Elevated CRP may indicate:
- Bacterial infection (often > 50 mg/L, sometimes > 200 mg/L)
- Viral infection (usually mild elevation, < 50 mg/L)
- Autoimmune diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, lupus)
- Tissue necrosis or injury
- Malignancy
- Post-surgical inflammation

CRP is useful for:
- Distinguishing bacterial from viral infection (higher in bacterial)
- Monitoring treatment response (decreases with effective therapy)
- Assessing disease severity in infections

### Limitations
- Non-specific (elevated in many conditions)
- Can be normal in early infection
- Affected by liver disease
- Not useful alone for diagnosis

## Procalcitonin

### Overview
Procalcitonin is a more specific marker for bacterial infection compared to CRP. It rises within 2-4 hours of bacterial infection and peaks at 24 hours.

### Normal Values
- Normal: < 0.1 ng/mL
- Low risk of bacterial infection: < 0.25 ng/mL
- Possible bacterial infection: 0.25–0.5 ng/mL
- Likely bacterial infection: > 0.5 ng/mL
- Severe bacterial infection/sepsis: > 2 ng/mL

### Clinical Use
- Helps differentiate bacterial from viral respiratory infections
- Guides antibiotic initiation and duration
- Prognostic marker in sepsis

## Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)

## Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)

### Overview
ESR measures the rate at which red blood cells settle in a tube. It is an older, less specific inflammatory marker that changes more slowly than CRP.

### Normal Values
- Men: 0–15 mm/hr (age < 50), 0–20 mm/hr (age > 50)
- Women: 0–20 mm/hr (age < 50), 0–30 mm/hr (age > 50)

### Elevated ESR
Causes include:
- Infection
- Autoimmune diseases (especially temporal arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica)
- Malignancy (especially multiple myeloma)
- Anemia
- Pregnancy
- Advanced age

# Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP) — Clinical Overview

Title: Community-Acquired Pneumonia Clinical Guide
Document Type: clinical_guideline

## Definition

Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is an acute infection of the pulmonary parenchyma acquired outside the hospital setting. It remains one of the most common infectious diseases and a significant cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide.

## Etiology

## Etiology

The most common pathogens include:
- Streptococcus pneumoniae (most frequent bacterial cause)
- Haemophilus influenzae
- Mycoplasma pneumoniae (common in younger adults)
- Chlamydophila pneumoniae
- Respiratory viruses (influenza, SARS-CoV-2, RSV)
- Legionella pneumophila (consider in severe cases)

## Clinical Presentation

Typical symptoms include:
- Cough (productive or non-productive)
- Fever or hypothermia
- Dyspnea (shortness of breath)
- Pleuritic chest pain
- Fatigue and malaise

Physical examination findings may include:
- Tachypnea (respiratory rate > 20/min)
- Tachycardia
- Decreased breath sounds
- Crackles or rales on auscultation
- Dullness to percussion over affected area
- Bronchial breathing

## Laboratory Findings

## Laboratory Findings

Common laboratory abnormalities:
- Elevated white blood cell count (WBC > 11,000/μL) — leukocytosis
- Elevated C-reactive protein (CRP)
- Elevated procalcitonin (supports bacterial etiology)
- Possible hypoxemia on arterial blood gas
- Elevated lactate in severe cases

## Imaging

Chest radiograph typically shows:
- Lobar consolidation (typical pneumonia)
- Interstitial or patchy infiltrates (atypical pneumonia)
- Air bronchograms
- Possible pleural effusion

## Differential Diagnosis

Conditions that may present similarly:
- Acute bronchitis
- Pulmonary embolism
- Congestive heart failure
- Lung malignancy
- Tuberculosis
- Hypersensitivity pneumonitis

## Severity Assessment

The CURB-65 score is commonly used:
- Confusion
- Urea > 7 mmol/L
- Respiratory rate ≥ 30/min
- Blood pressure < 90/60 mmHg
- Age ≥ 65 years

Each factor scores 1 point. Score 0-1: outpatient, 2: consider admission, 3-5: consider ICU.

## Complications

## Complications

- Parapneumonic effusion
- Empyema
- Lung abscess
- Sepsis
- Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)

# Renal Function Assessment — Clinical Overview

Title: Renal Function Assessment
Document Type: educational

## Creatinine

### Overview
Serum creatinine is a waste product of muscle metabolism filtered by the kidneys. It is one of the primary markers used to assess kidney function.

### Normal Values
- Men: 0.7–1.3 mg/dL (62–115 μmol/L)
- Women: 0.6–1.1 mg/dL (53–97 μmol/L)

### Elevated Creatinine

### Elevated Creatinine

Causes of elevated serum creatinine:
- Acute kidney injury (AKI)
- Chronic kidney disease (CKD)
- Dehydration
- Medications (ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, aminoglycosides)
- Obstruction of urinary tract
- Rhabdomyolysis
- High protein diet or muscle mass (mild elevation)
- Heart failure (reduced renal perfusion)

### Decreased Creatinine
- Low muscle mass
- Malnutrition
- Liver disease (decreased creatine production)

## Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)

### Normal Values
- 7–20 mg/dL

## Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)

### Normal Values
- 7–20 mg/dL

### Elevated BUN
Causes:
- Dehydration (prerenal azotemia) — BUN:Creatinine ratio > 20:1
- Kidney disease
- Heart failure
- GI bleeding
- High protein diet
- Catabolic states

## Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate (eGFR)

### Overview
eGFR is calculated from serum creatinine, age, sex, and race. It is the best overall indicator of kidney function.

### Staging of CKD by eGFR
- Stage 1: eGFR ≥ 90 (normal kidney function with other evidence of damage)
- Stage 2: eGFR 60–89 (mildly decreased)
- Stage 3a: eGFR 45–59 (mild to moderate decrease)
- Stage 3b: eGFR 30–44 (moderate to severe decrease)
- Stage 4: eGFR 15–29 (severely decreased)
- Stage 5: eGFR < 15 (kidney failure)

## Urinalysis

## Urinalysis

Key findings:
- Proteinuria: May indicate glomerular disease
- Hematuria: Infection, stones, malignancy, glomerulonephritis
- Casts: Red cell casts (glomerulonephritis), white cell casts (pyelonephritis), muddy brown casts (ATN)
- Specific gravity: Hydration status and concentrating ability

## Clinical Context

## Clinical Context

Renal function assessment should consider:
- Baseline kidney function
- Acute vs. chronic changes
- Medications affecting kidneys
- Volume status
- Comorbidities (diabetes, hypertension)
- Age-related decline in eGFR is common
